The diameter of the wide portion is double the diameter of the narrow portion.

hints: Notice the same tension $T$ pulls both ends, so the force is identical in the wide and narrow portions but the cross-sectional areas differ.
Recall tensile stress is $\text{stress} = F/A$ with $A = \pi d^2/4$, so doubling the diameter $d$ quadruples the area $A$.
Work out $A_{wide}/A_{narrow}$ from the factor of 2 in diameter, then use the inverse relationship between stress and area to form the required ratio.
walkthrough: The tensile force is the same everywhere in the bar, equal to $T$, while the cross-sectional area changes between the wide and narrow portions.
Use $\text{stress} = F/A = T/A$, so for the ratio: $\frac{\text{stress}_{wide}}{\text{stress}_{narrow}} = \frac{T/A_{wide}}{T/A_{narrow}} = \frac{A_{narrow}}{A_{wide}}$.
For circular section $A = \pi r^2 = \pi d^2/4$, so $A$ is proportional to $d^2$.

A.explanation: Stress is $T/A$ and the wide area is four times the narrow area, so the wide stress is one quarter of the narrow stress.

B.explanation: This uses diameter ratio directly for area, but area of a circle depends on $d^2$, not $d$.

C.explanation: This inverts the ratio, giving narrow to wide stress for diameter only without squaring.

D.explanation: This is the ratio of wide area to narrow area, which is the inverse of the stress ratio.
